narrative:
The 2026 Minnesota Twins entered the season with cautious optimism, and early returns were mixed at best. A rocky March (1-3) gave way to a losing April (13-15) filled with costly bullpen moments and defensive lapses that let opponents off the hook in close games. The high-leverage highlights of those opening weeks tell the story plainly: opponents capitalizing on Twins mistakes, with only Austin Martin's timely double and Ryan Jeffers' grand slam offering flashes of what the offense could be.

May and June brought little clarity. The team went 13-15 in each month, treading water in the AL Central while pitchers like Joe Ryan and relievers Eric Orze and Anthony Banda absorbed brutal, game-altering hits. A Bryan Reynolds two-run homer off Taylor Rogers on May 29 — one of the season's most damaging single plays by win probability — symbolized a bullpen that couldn't protect leads. Yet even in the muddle, Brooks Lee's clutch double and Kody Clemens' home run run showed the lineup had teeth. June ended on a sour note when Yordan Alvarez launched a grand slam off Ryan to effectively close out a tough Houston series.

July changed everything. The Twins caught fire at 15-9, their best month of the season, and the catalyst was unmistakable: Royce Lewis, returning and electrifying, delivered a go-ahead triple at the end of July that swung nearly a full win in probability, and Kody Clemens followed days later with the season's single most impactful play — a walk-off grand slam worth +0.927 WPA that sent Target Field into bedlam. For a few weeks, Minnesota looked like a team capable of making a postseason push.

August cooled those dreams fast. A 10-17 collapse erased the momentum built in July, and by September the Twins were playing out a complicated string, sitting at 77-85. The final month has offered individual bright spots — Royce Lewis driving in runs in early September, Walker Jenkins hitting his first home runs, and Travis Adams inducing a crucial double play — but the relief corps has continued to struggle, with A.J. Minter and Yoendrys Gómez surrendering critical late-game damage. With a below-.500 record and the calendar winding down, Minnesota's 2026 story is one of tantalizing potential interrupted by inconsistency, a team that showed its ceiling in July but couldn't sustain it.

chapters.title: Stumbling Out of the Gate
chapters.description: A rough March and losing April set a frustrating tone, with costly bullpen and defensive breakdowns undermining a lineup that flashed promise.

chapters.title: Treading Water
chapters.description: Minnesota spent May and early June grinding through .500 baseball, with damaging losses and sporadic offensive heroics keeping them from any real momentum.

chapters.title: Midsummer Sparks
chapters.description: Late June offered isolated bright moments — Clemens' home run, Jackson's clutch single — as the team searched for an identity before July's surge.

chapters.title: The July Explosion
chapters.description: Royce Lewis' return and Kody Clemens' grand slam headline a 15-9 month that gave Twins fans genuine reason to believe.

chapters.title: August Collapse and September Survival
chapters.description: A 10-17 August erased the playoff dream, and September has been a battle for pride, featuring young contributors but continued bullpen woes.
